subject: chemistry
title: Gibbs free energy and feasibility
key_idea: The **Gibbs free energy change**, ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, combines enthalpy and entropy. A reaction is feasible when ΔG is zero or negative. Temperature changes the balance. Feasible does not mean fast: a reaction with a negative ΔG may still not happen if its rate is too slow.

blocks.text: Enthalpy and entropy both affect whether a reaction can happen. The Gibbs equation puts them together in a single quantity measured in kJ mol⁻¹.

blocks.label: Gibbs free energy change
where: ΔG = free energy change, in kJ mol⁻¹
ΔH = enthalpy change of the system, in kJ mol⁻¹
ΔS = entropy change of the system, in kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (divide J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ by 1000)

items: TΔS is a temperature-dependent term. It becomes more important as the temperature rises.
Feasible (spontaneous) reaction: ΔG is zero or negative.
Not feasible: ΔG is positive.
−ΔG ÷ T is the total entropy change, so ΔG < 0 is the same as ΔS(total) > 0.
The units of ΔS must match ΔH. Convert J to kJ before using the equation.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS.
ΔG ≤ 0: the reaction is feasible.
Convert ΔS from J to kJ before using the equation.

blocks.text: Because T multiplies ΔS, the signs of ΔH and ΔS decide whether temperature can change the answer.

rows: At all temperatures: ΔG is always negative
At no temperature: ΔG is always positive
Only at low temperatures, where ΔH outweighs TΔS
Only at high temperatures, where TΔS outweighs ΔH

blocks.label: Temperature at which a reaction becomes feasible
where: T = the temperature at which ΔG = 0, in K

diagram.alt: Move the enthalpy change, entropy change and temperature to see the free energy change and the total entropy change.

inputs.label: Entropy change of the system, ΔS

blocks.text: Worked example: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g), with ΔH = +178 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = +160 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹.

items.text: Both ΔH and ΔS are positive, so the reaction is feasible above 1113 K.

diagram.alt: Practise finding the temperature at which a reaction becomes feasible from its enthalpy and entropy changes.
diagram.question: A reaction has ΔH = **{h} kJ mol⁻¹** and ΔS = **{s} J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹**. Calculate the temperature, in K, above which it becomes feasible.

items: Same signs for ΔH and ΔS: temperature decides feasibility.
At the changeover temperature, ΔG = 0 and T = ΔH ÷ ΔS.
Positive ΔH and ΔS: feasible at high T. Negative ΔH and ΔS: feasible at low T.

blocks.text: ΔG says whether a reaction can happen. It says nothing about how fast it happens, so it must be read together with the kinetics.

items: A negative ΔG means the reaction is thermodynamically feasible. It does not mean it will happen at a measurable rate.
Many feasible reactions have a high activation energy, so very few particles collide with enough energy. The reaction is too slow to see.
Example: diamond turning into graphite has a negative ΔG, but at room temperature it is far too slow.
A catalyst or a higher temperature can speed up a feasible reaction. A catalyst does not change ΔG.
A reaction with a positive ΔG at standard conditions may happen at a different temperature, or with conditions that are not standard.
The value of ΔG is calculated for standard conditions. Real conditions can give a different answer.
Negative ΔG: feasible, but no information about rate.
High activation energy can stop a feasible reaction.
A catalyst changes the rate, not ΔG.

checks.q: Calculate ΔG at 298 K for a reaction with ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS = −199 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. State whether it is feasible.
checks.a: ΔG = −92 − 298 × (−0.199) = −92 + 59.3 = −32.7 kJ mol⁻¹. ΔG is negative, so the reaction is feasible.

checks.q: Explain why the reaction in the previous question is not feasible at high temperatures.
checks.a: ΔS is negative, so −TΔS is positive and grows with temperature. At high temperatures it outweighs the negative ΔH and ΔG becomes positive.

checks.q: A reaction has a negative ΔG but does not occur at room temperature. Explain why.
checks.a: The reaction has a high activation energy, so it is too slow at room temperature. ΔG shows that it is feasible, not how fast it goes.

items: Explain that feasibility depends on TΔS as well as on ΔH, and do related calculations with the Gibbs equation.
Explain the limitations of ΔG predictions in terms of kinetics.

items: A reaction that is feasible (ΔG negative) has ln K positive, so K is large and the products are favoured.
A reaction that is not feasible (ΔG positive) has ln K negative, so K is small.
ΔG = 0 gives ln K = 0, so K = 1.
A reaction with a negative ΔG may not occur in practice because of kinetic factors, such as a high activation energy.
Derivation of ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is not required.
A reaction is feasible when ΔG is zero or negative.
Be able to calculate entropy changes from absolute entropy values, work out how ΔG varies with temperature, and find the temperature at which a reaction becomes feasible.
